items.prompt: This document is an author's adjudication of hostile referee findings on their own theory and experiments. The author is the judge of findings against their own work. Audit the adjudication for leniency: (a) verdicts of 'Partly valid', 'Invalid', 'Duplicate', 'minor' or 'did not bite' that let the author off when the finding is in fact valid, distinct, or serious; (b) 'Why' entries that restate the finding, change the subject, or promise a future experiment instead of answering; (c) concessions that are worded so the original claim quietly survives; (d) findings the tables mention but never rule on. Quote the row. Be specific: which verdict should change, to what, and why.

These two errata files retract or narrow claims from two experiments after a hostile review. Check whether the retractions are sufficient: for every 'what the experiment now claims' sentence, ask whether the conceded findings in the same file already undermine it. Find claims that survive in the errata only because they were reworded. Find internal inconsistencies between sections (a finding conceded in one section and relied on in another). Quote the exact sentences.

This document records an author accepting most findings of hostile referees against their own work. Your job is the opposite of the referees': find where the author conceded something that is actually wrong, or conceded more than the finding warranted. Referees overreach; authors under pressure over-concede. Look for: findings rated 'Valid' that rest on a misreading of the document under attack; 'fatal' ratings for what is a fixable wording issue; concessions that contradict other concessions; places where a stated pre-registered limit is treated as concealment. Quote the row and say what the correct verdict is.

The errata sketch a third experiment (section 10 of the errata; also referred to across the adjudication): equal access to defect records for both processes, matched search operator and budget, one process uses per-record credit and the other must collapse the records to a scalar, scramble applied to both, a world law fixed before the rule language is written, closedness measured against a sensory ceiling. Attack this design before it is built. Is the itemised-versus-scalar contrast also trivial by construction? What would a result in either direction fail to show? What confounds survive? What does 'a world law fixed before the language' require in practice, and can the author, who knows the law, meet it? Propose the sharpest version of the experiment that could actually fail.
